meta.title: Czech A1
meta.subtitle: 1,213 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Czech → English (see the Czech, recall the meaning) and English → Czech (see an English meaning, recall the Czech). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1,213 words and expressions for level A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM: 1,162 of them are the A1 entries of the official word list of the Czech language exam for permanent residence — the Soupis lexikálních jednotek published by the National Pedagogical Institute of the Czech Republic (NPI ČR) with its reference description of Czech for levels A1 and A2 — that an English dictionary can teach. The list's grammatical patterns ("čekat na", "chtít + infinitive") and the phrases written with a blank or a choice of endings are not cards. 2 of them are verbs the list names only inside a collocation (dělat sport, označit křížkem), taught on their own. The other 51 are short grammatical words — personal and possessive pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions and numbers — which the list leaves to the reference description's grammar chapters rather than its word list: they were added by Folio, as the commonest such words of everyday Czech that are on neither the A1 nor the A2 list, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles. They are Folio's addition, not part of the official list. The cards are ordered by how often each word is met in that frequency list, each word counted over all its forms, so the commonest come first; the 20 multi-word expressions, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Czech changes the endings of its nouns, adjectives and verbs, and stems change with them, so each card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 664 nouns show their gender, three cases of the singular and two of the plural — pes: masculine animate, psa, psovi, psem, psi, psů. 193 verbs show their aspect and its partner, the forms for já (I), on (he) and oni (they) and the past of on — jít: imperfective, jdu, jde, jdou, šel — a perfective verb's present forms being its future. 55 adjectives show their comparative and superlative. 9 pronouns show their cases. A reflexive verb is taught as the list writes it, with its se or si (bát se, dát si); where the dictionary's meaning says only that a sense is reflexive, it is marked (se/si). Real example sentences come with 1,120 of the 1,213 entries, three apiece for 976, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Word list: NPI ČR, Soupis lexikálních jednotek A1, A2 (cestina-pro-cizince.cz) — the words only. Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
